content: To minimize the risk of developing additional drug resistance, it is critical to avoid adding single tuberculosis (TB) medications to the treatment regimen of patients who remain smearor culture-positive after two months of treatment, those who do not show favorable clinical responses, or those without recent drug susceptibility testing (DST) results. As with any TB medication or treatment regimen, safety precautions must be in place to promptly identify and manage any serious adverse events (SAEs). Close clinical monitoring is essential for all patients receiving this regimen, with particular attention to liver function tests due to the hepatotoxic potential of prolonged pyrazinamide use. Monthly testing of aspartate aminotransferase (AST or SGOT) levels is recommended for all patients, if resources allow. If resources are limited, monthly monitoring should focus on high-risk patients, such as those co-infected with viral hepatitis or with a history of heavy alcohol use. For pediatric patients, it is crucial to adhere to the recommended doses of ethambutol to prevent toxicity, such as retrobulbar neuritis. Early signs of ethambutol toxicity can be assessed in older children through red-green color discrimination tests. Monitoring for retrobulbar neuritis should be initiated when appropriate. When designing longer multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) regimens, the inclusion of Group A agents (fluoroquinolones like levofloxacin or moxifloxacin, bedaquiline, and linezolid) is strongly recommended due to their high effectiveness. If only one or two Group A agents can be used, both Group B agents (clofazimine and cycloserine or terizidone) should be included. If the regimen cannot be composed using agents from Groups A and B alone, Group C agents (such as ethambutol, delamanid, pyrazinamide, carbapenems like imipenem-cilastatin or meropenem, amikacin, ethionamide or prothionamide, and p-aminosalicylic acid) may be added to complete the regimen. Kanamycin and capreomycin are no longer recommended for MDR-TB treatment due to their association with poorer outcomes. Levofloxacin or moxifloxacin should be included in longer MDR-TB regimens, as they are strongly recommended with moderate certainty of effectiveness. Bedaquiline is also strongly recommended for patients aged 18 years or older, while its use in children aged 6–17 years is conditionally recommended based on limited data. Linezolid is strongly recommended for inclusion in longer MDR-TB regimens, with evidence suggesting that its use for at least six months improves effectiveness, although toxicity may limit its duration. Clofazimine and cycloserine or terizidone are conditionally recommended as second-choice agents. Ethambutol, delamanid, pyrazinamide, and amikacin may be included in specific circumstances, but their use is conditional and based on very low certainty of evidence. If amikacin is unavailable, streptomycin may be considered under similar conditions. Ethionamide or prothionamide and p-aminosalicylic acid should only be used when better options are unavailable, as their effectiveness is limited to regimens without newer agents like bedaquiline, linezolid, clofazimine, or delamanid. The World Health Organization (WHO) recommends that all patients diagnosed with rifampicin-resistant TB (RR-TB) or MDR-TB be placed on an appropriate treatment regimen. The design of longer MDR-TB regimens should ideally include at least four effective agents during the intensive phase and at least three agents during the continuation phase. The use of high-dose isoniazid and ethambutol may be considered to strengthen the regimen further, but only when susceptibility is confirmed. The WHO guidelines emphasize the importance of individualized treatment regimens based on reliable DST results. Longer MDR-TB regimens typically last 20 months or more and may be standardized or tailored to the patient’s needs. The inclusion of sufficient effective agents is critical to maximize the likelihood of relapse-free cure while minimizing toxicity. The use of injectable agents is expected to decrease in future regimens, with a shift toward all-oral regimens. For pediatric patients, evidence from adult studies is often extrapolated due to limited data. Bedaquiline and delamanid have been conditionally recommended for use in children, with specific age restrictions and dosing considerations. The safety and efficacy of these medications in younger children require further study.
